summary:
Bahrain decriminalised same-sex sexual activity in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era statute, and is the only Gulf state that does not explicitly penalise same-sex intimacy. No statute criminalises transgender expression. The 1976 penal code sets 21 as the age of adulthood for consensual same-sex acts, and the country has no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics.

Decriminalisation has not removed exposure. Articles 324, 329 and 350 of the penal code, covering indecency and debauchery, carry three months to two years' imprisonment, fines of up to 200 dinars, and deportation for non-Bahrainis, and the government has applied them to people suspected of being LGBTQI+ or of cross-dressing. Documented cases include a 2009 one-month sentence imposed on a man who wore an abaya and carried a purse in public, a 2011 police raid on a party described as a same-sex wedding, and the arrest of nine cross-dressers at a hotel discotheque party in Manama on New Year's Eve charged with public debauchery. In February 2024 the Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation, extending the framework under which such charges are brought.

Entry is a distinct exposure point. The Interior Minister has stated that suspected effeminate homosexuals are barred from entering Bahrain through airport checks, and pending bills have proposed expressly banning LGBTQ foreigners from entry or residency permits. In September 2013 the Gulf Cooperation Countries agreed to discuss a proposal to establish testing to bar gay foreigners, though officials later backtracked. A foreign government's official guidance records that arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare.

Legal gender recognition is refused by the courts. In a May 2023 judgment a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and for gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia, and refused his request for a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination. Courts require medical documentation of a sex change operation or of medical necessity before a legal gender marker is changed, and a 2023 ruling held sex-reassignment procedures to be against Islamic law where a case is considered solely related to gender dysphoria, limiting eligibility to people with intersex traits. Article 330 of the penal code additionally mandates that anyone charged with prostitution or 'fujoor' be taken to a hospital for sexually transmitted disease testing and potentially relocated to a medical facility.

Protection machinery is thin. Article 309 of the penal code protects religious groups but does not extend equivalent protection to LGBTQ people, and hate speech against LGBTQ people remains widespread without legal consequence. False accusations of homosexuality are used to discredit and bully government critics and protesters, including human rights advocate Nabeel Rajab and demonstrators at Pearl Square in 2011.

No LGBTQ-specific facilities, shelters or community organisations operate in the country. The US Department of State reports that no LGBTQ-related organisation is approved, and ILGA concludes that it is improbable that any sexual- or gender-diversity group would be registered, because the body controlling association registration may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order.
tangentialFactors:
Source conflict over the basic legal position remains unresolved. Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada research response BHR105575.E, published in August 2016 and covering 2011 to July 2016, reports that 'according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain', citing Canadian and Gulf News material. That reading contradicts the 1976 decriminalisation recorded by Wikipedia's ILGA-sourced entry, Outright International and the 2023 US State Department report, and the inventory offers no material that reconciles the two.

Sourcing for this jurisdiction is structurally constrained. Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for a decade, including United Nations human-rights bodies and Amnesty International, so local media often serve as the only available source for conditions inside the country.

Media hostility is documented and carries no legal consequence. A widely viewed caricature published in Albilad on 3 August 2024 depicted a pride-flag roll of toilet paper captioned 'the correct place', and the Gulf Daily News has run articles on female homosexuality in girls' high schools.

Several legislative proposals remain pending rather than enacted, and the inventory does not establish their current status: an October 2021 bill that would have criminalised promoting or inviting others to homosexual gatherings with up to five years' imprisonment, the entry and residency bans on LGBTQ foreigners, and bills instructing teachers to identify warning signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing in children.
localsOnly:
Sexuality and gender expression are treated as a school-discipline matter. In response to parliamentary questions about lesbianism in schools, Assistant Under-Secretary for Educational Services Khalid Al Alawi stated that the Education Ministry is not responsible for addressing sexuality, that it is parents' job, and that 'the public shouldn't make a big deal out of this problem because it does not exist', while adding that students whose appearance is contrary to school values should be disciplined.

Enforcement reaches schools directly. On 14 February 2024 the Ministry of Education referred a private school's administration and its entire board to investigation and dismissed its general manager after a video showed students performing a scene in which two male students pretended to propose to each other. A 2022 incident, in which a private school distributed material perceived as promoting homosexuality, also triggered calls for stricter laws.

Pending bills would instruct children's teachers in warning signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing so that children can be punished, and an October 2021 bill would have criminalised promoting or inviting others to homosexual gatherings with up to five years' imprisonment.

Organised community life is effectively unavailable: no LGBTQ-specific facilities, shelters or community organisations exist, no LGBTQ-related organisation is approved, and the body controlling association registration may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order, which ILGA treats as making registration of a sexual- or gender-diversity group improbable.
blindOutOfScope:
The conflict between the two readings of the basic legal position is unresolved in the available material: a foreign country's refugee research body reported in 2016, citing press sources, that same-sex relations are illegal here, while an international rights organisation, an international advocacy organisation and a foreign government's 2023 country report all record decriminalisation in 1976. Nothing in the inventory reconciles them.

Enforcement frequency is not quantified. The only figure available is a foreign government's characterisation that arrests for such behaviour are relatively rare, with no arrest statistics, prosecution data or sentencing records supplied.

The status of the pending bills is not sourced. Whether the entry and residency bans, the promotion bill and the school warning-sign bills were enacted, lapsed or remain before the legislature is unresolved in this inventory, as is the current effect of the moral legislation adopted by the national legislature in February 2024.

No sourced information was found on how authorities classify trans detainees for housing, on whether a gender marker change is available on a passport or national identity document, or on conditions of detention for gender-nonconforming people. The 2013 proposal by a regional bloc of neighbouring states to test and bar gay foreigners was publicly backtracked, and its subsequent fate is not established here.
